newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Boss hails Boss at Swedish "Nobel Music Prize".
newsitem.headline: Boss hails Boss at Swedish "Nobel Music Prize".

text.p: One "boss" paid tribute to another "boss" on Monday when U.S. President Bill Clinton sent a message congratulating rock legend Bruce Springsteen for winning the 1997 Polar Prize, dubbed the Nobel Prize for musicians.

"In the U.S. of A. Bruce Springsteen is known as "The Boss." Well back in Washington I've got a boss too and this is what he has to say," U.S. ambassador to Sweden Thomas Siebert told a gathering including the Swedish royal family and Springsteen.
In the message, Clinton paid tribute to the 47-year-old singer's "great poetic spirit and deep respect for the roots of your musical heritage."
"You always seem to open new doors for us," the ambassador quoted Clinton as saying.
Springsteen, known as "The Boss" to millions of fans around the world, was jointly awarded the one million crown ($125,000) prize with choral conductor Eric Ericson.

Springsteen was to fly to Vienna on Tuesday where he is to start the final, 20-date leg of a world tour that has lasted a year and in which Springsteen forsakes his famous driving rock for his latest, acoustic works.
The prize was established by Stikkan Anderson, former manager of pop group Abba, and is awarded to people, groups or institutions which have acted decisively in the world of music.
It is generally shared between a pop singer and a classical musician. Previous winners include Paul McCartney, Joni Mitchell, Elton John, Quincy Jones and Dizzy Gillespie.

Ericson and Springsteen received the award from Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in central Stockholm. Springsteen, 47, swapped his trademark jeans and open-necked shirt for a tie-less tuxedo for the occasion.
Ericson, 78, created Sweden's first professional choral group in 1946.
